name: Webdriver Torso
title: 80,000 Videos of Rectangles, and Nobody Knew Why
claims: Webdriver Torso is a YouTube automated performance testing account that became famous in 2014 | 1
The channel began uploading in September 2013, with simple slides accompanied by beeps | 1
There were over 80,000 videos, each 11 seconds long | 2
Videos uploaded as often as every two minutes at peak | 2
Almost all videos show blue and red rectangles moving in seemingly random directions | 1, 2
Soundtrack is varying sine wave tones / computer-generated tones | 1, 2
Example titles tmpAZWIOG, tmpXsjor2, tmpvRXNJM | 2
Hypotheses included a numbers station, extraterrestrial contact, and a Cicada 3301 recruitment program | 1
Hypotheses included encoded spy messages and alien contact | 2
The Daily Dot, the BBC and The Guardian covered the mystery | 2
A BoingBoing user claimed to have seen very similar images on a set-top box at a Google conference about automation | 2
The same user tracked down the slides, which showed the test videos were slightly different, according to The Guardian | 2
Three videos do not follow the standard format | 1
tmpRkRL85 plays normally until the red rectangle becomes a dancing silhouette of Rick Astley in the second half | 1, 2
Title possibly stands for "Temporary Rick Roll 1985" or "Template Rickroll 1985" | 1
00014 is footage recorded in Paris of the Eiffel Tower lit up at night | 1
At the end of 00014 the camera is put down and the Webdriver Torso Facebook page is visible for a few frames | 1
0.455442373793 is viewable only in France, costs 1.99 euros, payable only with a French credit card | 1
It shows an Aqua Teen Hunger Force episode, dubbed in Spanish (source 1) or French (source 2); sources disagree | 1, 2
The channel at one time commented "Matei is highly intelligent"; several people named Matei were suspected; the comment was later removed | 1
A blogger took findings to The Daily Dot and deserves perhaps more credit than anyone for solving the puzzle | 2
Webdriver Torso belongs to a network of accounts called "ytuploadtestpartner_torso" | 1, 2
Other accounts with similar videos were found; many were pulled or made private after the investigation was published | 1, 2
A Google+ account linked to a Facebook page and a Twitter account, both since taken down | 2
The Facebook page mentioned a Google employee who was friends with another Google employee based in Zurich, whose first name was Matei, a name also mentioned in the Eiffel Tower clip | 1, 2
The blogger compared scenes in pulled videos with Zurich Google office photos and noted matching lamps and desk phones | 1, 2
Searching "Webdriver Torso" on Google makes the logo look like a Webdriver Torso video; a Doodle sometimes prevents it | 1
A YouTube Easter egg exists for the search | 2
The Android L developer builds' version Easter egg references Webdriver Torso | 1
YouTube's official statement, quoted in full, referencing Never Gonna Give You Up | 1, 2
The videos test YouTube video quality: they are uploaded and compared with the originals to see how much quality was lost | 1, 2
The vanished accounts were also Google test accounts, including one called Timmy Tester; Google wouldn't say what they tested | 2
The channel going viral was an accident, and Google played along | 2
Google's explanation did not explain the humorous references (Aqua Teen, Rick Astley, Eiffel Tower) | 1
The identity of "Matei" is unknown | 1
Simple shapes and tones make comparison easy (presented as presumption, not as sourced fact) | none, inference
The Facebook page and desk-phone evidence pointed to an office (inference from matching photos) | 1, 2

sources.title: Google and the accidental mystery of Webdriver Torso
